summary.text: For \(k>59\), set \(n=2k+1\); each potentially nonzero matrix entry corresponds to two primes whose sum is \(2n=4k+2\), so failure of such a decomposition makes the entire matrix zero and contradicts the assumed nonzero determinant. The remaining cases \(1\le k\le59\) are settled by an explicit finite list of prime decompositions.

full_proof.text:
Let \(A(n)\) denote the determinant in the statement. Thus, for \(n\geq 1\), let \(M_n\) be the \(n\times n\) matrix whose rows and columns are indexed by \(i,j\in\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}\), with
\[
 (M_n)_{ij}=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&\text{if both }n+i-j\text{ and }n+j-i\text{ are prime},\\
 0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Then \(A(n)=\det(M_n)\). (The two displayed differences are positive: for example, since \(j\leq n-1\), we have \(n+i-j\geq1\), and similarly for the other one. Thus there is no ambiguity between ordinary integer subtraction and subtraction in the natural numbers.)

Assume the conjectured nonvanishing statement
\[
\tag{H}
\text{for every odd integer }n>120,\qquad A(n)\neq0.
\]
We prove that, for every positive integer \(k\), the number \(4k+2\) is a sum of two primes.

We first establish the elementary fact connecting a failure of Goldbach at \(2n\) with the determinant \(A(n)\).

**Matrix-vanishing lemma.** If \(n>0\) and there are no primes \(p,q\) satisfying \(p+q=2n\), then \(A(n)=0\).

Indeed, fix any row and column indices \(i,j\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\), and set
\[
 p_{ij}=n+i-j,\qquad q_{ij}=n+j-i.
\]
As observed above, both are positive integers. Moreover, cancellation gives
\[
 p_{ij}+q_{ij}=(n+i-j)+(n+j-i)=2n.
\]
Consequently, if both \(p_{ij}\) and \(q_{ij}\) were prime, they would give a representation of \(2n\) as a sum of two primes, contrary to the assumption. Hence at least one of them is not prime, so the definition of the matrix gives \((M_n)_{ij}=0\). This applies to every pair \((i,j)\), and therefore \(M_n\) is the zero matrix. Because \(n>0\), its determinant is zero (equivalently, every term in the determinant expansion contains a zero matrix entry). Thus \(A(n)=0\), proving the lemma.

There is a small finite range which must be handled separately because hypothesis (H) applies only when its odd argument is greater than \(120\). For every \(k\) with \(1\leq k\leq59\), the following table supplies a decomposition of \(4k+2\) into two primes:
\[
\begin{array}{c|r@{\;}c@{\;}l||c|r@{\;}c@{\;}l}
k&\multicolumn{3}{c||}{4k+2}&k&\multicolumn{3}{c}{4k+2}\\ \hline
 1&  6&=&3+3&31&126&=&13+113\\
 2& 10&=&3+7&32&130&=&3+127\\
 3& 14&=&3+11&33&134&=&3+131\\
 4& 18&=&5+13&34&138&=&7+131\\
 5& 22&=&3+19&35&142&=&3+139\\
 6& 26&=&3+23&36&146&=&7+139\\
 7& 30&=&7+23&37&150&=&11+139\\
 8& 34&=&3+31&38&154&=&3+151\\
 9& 38&=&7+31&39&158&=&7+151\\
10& 42&=&5+37&40&162&=&5+157\\
11& 46&=&3+43&41&166&=&3+163\\
12& 50&=&3+47&42&170&=&3+167\\
13& 54&=&7+47&43&174&=&7+167\\
14& 58&=&5+53&44&178&=&5+173\\
15& 62&=&3+59&45&182&=&3+179\\
16& 66&=&5+61&46&186&=&5+181\\
17& 70&=&3+67&47&190&=&11+179\\
18& 74&=&3+71&48&194&=&3+191\\
19& 78&=&5+73&49&198&=&5+193\\
20& 82&=&3+79&50&202&=&3+199\\
21& 86&=&3+83&51&206&=&7+199\\
22& 90&=&7+83&52&210&=&11+199\\
23& 94&=&5+89&53&214&=&3+211\\
24& 98&=&19+79&54&218&=&7+211\\
25&102&=&5+97&55&222&=&11+211\\
26&106&=&3+103&56&226&=&3+223\\
27&110&=&3+107&57&230&=&3+227\\
28&114&=&5+109&58&234&=&5+229\\
29&118&=&5+113&59&238&=&5+233\\
30&122&=&13+109&&&&
\end{array}
\]
Every summand displayed in this table is prime. This is an entirely finite check: all the summands are at most \(233\), and trial division by the primes \(2,3,5,7,11,13\) suffices, since \(\sqrt{233}<16\). The displayed additions also directly verify each equality. Hence the desired conclusion holds for \(1\leq k\leq59\).

It remains to consider \(k>59\), so \(k\geq60\). Define
\[
 n=2k+1.
\]
Then \(n\) is odd, and
\[
 n=2k+1\geq 2\cdot60+1=121>120.
\]
Thus hypothesis (H) applies and yields
\[
\tag{1} A(n)\neq0.
\]
Also,
\[
\tag{2} 2n=2(2k+1)=4k+2.
\]
Suppose, for contradiction, that \(4k+2\) is not a sum of two primes. By (2), this says precisely that there are no primes \(p,q\) with \(p+q=2n\). Since \(n>0\), the matrix-vanishing lemma then gives
\[
 A(n)=0,
\]
contradicting (1). Therefore such primes \(p,q\) must exist, and by (2) they satisfy
\[
 4k+2=p+q.
\]

Combining this argument for \(k\geq60\) with the explicit finite table for \(1\leq k\leq59\), we conclude that every positive integer \(k\) admits primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
4k+2=p+q.
\]
This proves the claimed implication.
